title: 3D high-frequency ultrasound of the mouse colon to monitor tumor development
protocol: Anesthetize the mouse using i.p. injection of Ketamine 80 mg/kg body weight and Xylazine 8 mg/kg body weight.
Or, anesthetize the mouse by placing it in a chamber with a constant flow of 2–3 l/min 2-3% Isoflurane in medical air for induction.
Transfer the animal to a heated imaging pad after induction.
Gently tape the paws to ECG electrodes to monitor vital signs during imaging.
Apply ECG electrode gel if necessary to establish electrical contact.
Place the mouse’s nose into the Isoflurane/air nozzle and reduce Isoflurane concentration to 0.5–1%.
Adjust Isoflurane concentration if the animal shows signs of arousal or deep anesthesia.
Apply protective eye ointment to the mouse.
Remove hair from a ventral area rostral to the anus and as far as the xiphoid process using an electric hair clipper followed by hair removal cream.
Clean the skin carefully with physiological saline solution or water after hair removal.
Apply US gel generously to the abdomen.
Ensure the gel is free of air bubbles.
Carefully lower the transducer under US guidance towards the lower abdomen until structures below the abdominal musculature are visible.
Fill a 1 ml syringe with US gel, ensuring it remains connected if using a Luer-Lok syringe.
Connect the syringe to the plastic feeding tube.
Push out a small amount of US gel to moisten the tip of the tube.
Carefully insert the tube into the anus while applying soft pressure on the plunger.
Ensure the tube is visible in the live US image and adjust the imaging depth or transducer position if necessary.
Inject US gel to carefully inflate the lumen.
Count the number of tumors by recording a video loop from the rectum rostrally.
Move the scanning table manually towards the investigator to image the colon completely.
Tilt the imaging table or apply gentle manual pressure on the abdomen to adjust for overlying anatomical structures, bends in the colon, or inconsistent fillings with intraluminal contrast.
In male mice, tilt the imaging table to obtain an oblique view when the testes and penis impair the view of the most distal portion of the colon.
Use a 38 mm tube to inflate and image the area where tumors predominantly arise in the model used.
Switch to Color Doppler mode once the transducer is positioned over a tumor.
Observe vessels with flow towards the transducer colored red.
Note vessels with flow away from the transducer are colored blue.
Use Power-Doppler for higher sensitivity in signal detection.
Employ the Vevo probe MS550D for Doppler imaging.
Acquire B-mode images using the same Vevo probe MS550D.
Switch between Doppler mode and B-mode to obtain optimal positioning of the transducer.
Identify non-vascularized tissue such as necrotic areas by lack of Doppler signal.
Control anesthesia depth tightly for reliable inter- and intra-individual comparisons of blood flow and vessel density.
Use isoflurane instead of ketamine/xylazine for better control over hemodynamic conditions.
Monitor heart rate >450 beats/min and respiratory rate >100 breaths/min as standard parameters for C57BL/6J and FVB/NJ mice.
Adjust technical settings consistently between individual measurements.
Save and reload all preferences in the imaging system for consistency.
Use respiratory gating when acquiring Doppler images to reduce artifacts.
Perform image averaging to further decrease artifacts, increasing acquisition time as needed.
Visualize tumor vasculature and blood flow velocity using color or power Doppler.
Select pulsed-wave \(PW) Doppler from the Color Doppler window.
Display a scout window to locate the region of interest for PW measurements.
Adjust the beam angle to match the flow direction of the vessel of interest.
Acquire 3D volumetric data using µUS.
Compute the z dimension using a 3D-motor attached to the imaging probe.
Set the z-axis length typically between 2–10 mm, including the axial tumor diameter from proximal to distal borders.
Adjust physiological settings to avoid breathing artifacts in 3D images.
Ensure steady 3D-images of tumors of different sizes.
